paper_id: Detecting Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks by
evidence: We used a convolutional neural network (CNN) with two convolutional and two fully connected layers for prediction with the MNIST dataset.
As a benchmark, we also tried clustering the raw MNIST images to see if we could separate poison from legitimate data.
Both accuracy and F1 score are nearly 100% for every class.
we applied each method to activation clusters obtained from both poisoned and clean versions of MNIST, LISA, and Rotten Tomatoes models
unresolved: No seed count or repetition count for training runs is ever stated; each experiment (MNIST, LISA, Rotten Tomatoes) appears to be a single run, so n_seeds is left null rather than assumed to be 1.

n_models counted as 3 (MNIST CNN with 2 conv + 2 FC layers, LISA variant of Simonyan and Zisserman's Architecture A, Rotten Tomatoes text CNN from Britz/Kim) -- these are the classifiers the AC detection method is applied to, not competing detection methods.

n_eval_types counted as 6 (detection Accuracy, detection F1 score, ExRe score, relative cluster-size comparison, silhouette score, backdoor-repair test error before/after retraining). The gap statistic is mentioned as attempted for cluster-count comparison but reported as 'largely unsuccessful' and not tabulated, so it was not counted as a reported eval type.

n_baselines = 1: raw-pixel 2-means clustering (no activation extraction) on MNIST only, used as a benchmark against AC; no experimental comparison to other published backdoor-detection methods (e.g. Liu et al. fine-pruning) is run in this paper, only discussed in related work.
No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests appear anywhere in the results; all reported numbers (Tables 1-4) are single point-estimate percentages.
